theory.title: Theory and what to observe
theory.rle: RLE replaces runs of equal bytes with (count, value); it gains little on ordinary audio.
theory.huffman: Canonical Huffman gives frequent symbols short codes and derives code lengths from the histogram; nothing is lost.
theory.delta: The first-order predictor codes differences between adjacent samples; the smaller range makes Huffman more compact.
theory.companding: μ-law and A-law (G.711) compress amplitude logarithmically; 8 bits sound acceptable but are not bit-exact.
theory.mdct: A windowed MDCT with TDAC turns the signal into coefficients; uniform quantization under a bit budget produces playback-friendly error.

lanes.heading: Independent lane coding
lanes.body: Each lane gets its own codec and quantization settings. Real MP3 and AAC encoders often share side information across channels (joint stereo) to spend fewer bits; this lab keeps the lanes independent to make the trade-off visible.

observe.title: What to observe
observe.lossless: RLE, Huffman and delta+Huffman must show “bit-exact ✓”; μ-law, A-law and MDCT must not.
observe.entropy: Compare the lossless size with entropy; the coder approaches the theoretical bound.
observe.bitrate: In MDCT, sweep the bitrate and watch SNR/PSNR against bitrate.
observe.sparsity: MDCT coefficient sparsity shows how much quantization zeroes out.
observe.body: Read the size, bitrate, and quality numbers together. A lossless result must decode bit-exactly, while a lossy result is judged by the trade between bitrate and measured or heard distortion.

theory.title: Editing the spectrum and returning to time

inverse.heading: Inverse DFT
inverse.body: The editor changes selected bins of one frame, then runs the inverse transform. The result is real only when the edited spectrum obeys Hermitian symmetry. Otherwise the IFFT is complex and the player keeps the real part.

hermitian.heading: Hermitian symmetry
hermitian.body: For a real signal, bin N−k is the conjugate of bin k. Editing magnitude or phase independently can break that rule; the toggle shows the consequence instead of hiding it.

lanes.heading: Per-lane spectra
lanes.body: Hermitian symmetry and the edit list belong to one lane at a time. Independent editing can break the stereo relationship the original recording carried; using the same edits on both lanes keeps them aligned.

gibbs.heading: Sharp masks ring
gibbs.body: A brick-wall band edit is a sudden discontinuity in frequency. Its time-domain result has ripples near the edges: the Gibbs phenomenon. Smooth transitions trade sharpness for less ringing.

fftview.capNotice: Analysis is capped at {{samples}} samples; shrink the selection to cover it all.
fftview.error: The spectrum could not be computed.
fftview.empty: A non-empty analysis frame is required.

axis.phaseNote: Bins below {{threshold}} are masked: their phase is numerical noise.

benchmark.title: FFT benchmark
benchmark.note: Wall-clock times are machine-dependent; accuracy is the stable comparison. fft.js is used only for this benchmark.

butterfly.title: Cooley–Tukey butterfly
butterfly.error: Butterfly steps could not be computed.
butterfly.note: The input is bit-reversed before stage 1; each butterfly adds and subtracts the twiddled odd input.

dft.heading: Discrete Fourier transform
dft.body: The DFT compares the frame with complex sinusoids at N equally spaced frequencies. Bin k is the projection on e^{j2πkn/N}; the magnitude says how much, and the phase says where in the cycle.

window.heading: Windows and leakage
window.body: A rectangular window truncates abruptly and spreads energy into side lobes. Smooth windows lower leakage at the cost of a wider main lobe. Compare the window table to see this trade-off directly.

phase.heading: Phase is fragile
phase.body: Phase under a magnitude threshold is mostly numerical noise. The plot masks those bins; phase differences between nearby bins are more meaningful than absolute wrapped values.

amFm.overmodulation: The modulation index exceeds 1, so the envelope inverts (overmodulation).
amFm.amHint: AM: x(t) = A (1 + m sin(2πfm t)) sin(2πfc t).
amFm.fmHint: FM: x(t) = A sin(2πfc t + β sin(2πfm t)), with β = Δf / fm.

fourier.hint: More harmonics sharpen the edges; the Gibbs overshoot stays near 8.95 %.

fourier.heading: Building waves from sinusoids
fourier.body: Any periodic signal can be written as a sum of harmonics at integer multiples of f0. The generator's Fourier tab adds them one by one; the shape approaches the target as the harmonic count grows.

gibbs.heading: Gibbs ringing
gibbs.body: A truncated Fourier series cannot reproduce a jump exactly. The partial sum overshoots the edge by about 9% of the jump, no matter how many terms you add; only the ripple width shrinks.

preview.heading: Preview is not the file
preview.body: The preview draws a bucket envelope, not every sample. Check the sample count and duration, and remember that the loaded source is capped at 300 s and 96 kHz.

stft.heading: Short-time Fourier transform
stft.body: The spectrogram splits the signal into overlapping frames, applies a window, and computes a DFT per frame. Each column is a spectrum; colour encodes magnitude in dB. The hop controls how often the spectrum is measured.

resolution.heading: Time–frequency trade-off
resolution.body: A longer window gives finer frequency resolution but blurs short events; a shorter window does the opposite. The hop sets time spacing, while zero-padding only interpolates the displayed spectrum.

theory.title: Speed, resampling, and the phase vocoder

resample.heading: Tape-style resampling
resample.body: Playing the same samples faster multiplies pitch and tempo together. Resampling by r changes the duration by 1/r and every frequency by r; it is the simplest speed control and the easiest to hear.

vocoder.heading: Pitch-preserving time stretch
vocoder.body: The phase vocoder keeps the frame rate but advances the synthesis grid at a different rate. It accumulates phase from frame to frame so frequency stays put while duration changes; transient smearing is the usual artifact.

reverse.heading: Reverse is not reverb
reverse.body: Time reversal flips the sample order. Magnitude stays the same, phase is conjugated, and attacks become decays. Reverb, by contrast, convolves with a room impulse response.

lanes.heading: Stereo lanes
lanes.body: In both mode, each lane runs its own speed transform. Speed, mode, pitch shift and range are shared; reverse is per lane. Independent phase-vocoder lanes can drift in phase and move the stereo image, so check the result against mono when comparing.

observe.title: What to observe
observe.aliasing: Turn the anti-alias filter off and lower the target rate: a tone above the new Nyquist appears at a different frequency.
observe.dither: At low bit depth, dither replaces correlated quantization distortion with a steady noise floor.
observe.snr: Each extra bit adds about 6 dB of SNR; compare the measured value with the theoretical line.

nyquist.heading: Nyquist condition
nyquist.body: Sampling stores the signal at discrete instants. If the input contains energy above half the sample rate, those components fold back to lower frequencies and become indistinguishable from real content. The anti-alias filter must run before decimation.

alias.heading: Alias frequency
alias.body: A sine at f above Nyquist appears at the folded frequency f_alias. With the filter off you can hear the tone move down as the rate falls; switching the filter on removes the out-of-band energy before it can fold.

quantization.heading: Quantization and SNR
quantization.body: Reducing bit depth rounds every sample to a coarser grid. The step size grows, the error power grows, and the signal-to-noise ratio falls. Dither trades a little noise for the removal of correlated quantization distortion.

lanes.heading: Stereo lanes
lanes.body: Both lanes share the target rate and anti-alias filter because those fix the output grid. Bit depth and dither are per lane, so the measured SNR can differ between channels.

observe.title: What to observe
observe.truncate: A shorter truncation widens the main lobe and raises the bin width Δf = fs / N.
observe.zeroPad: Zero-padding adds no new information: it samples the same spectrum more densely, so the main-lobe width stays the same.
observe.tradeoff: A signal that is narrow in time is wide in frequency (time–bandwidth uncertainty).
observe.scale: Time scaling moves the spectrum inversely: x(at) has spectrum |a|⁻¹ X(f/a).
observe.periodic: Periodic extension produces spectral lines at multiples of 1/T.
observe.scaleNote: Time scaling deliberately has no anti-alias filter. For the filtered comparison, use the sampling lab (F03).
observe.units: Energy and average power are amplitude-squared values; for normalized audio in [−1, 1] the unit is full-scale².

energy.heading: Energy and average power
energy.body: Duration and support describe where a signal exists; energy and power describe how much it carries. A finite-energy pulse has zero average power over infinite time, while a periodic signal is a power signal.

resolution.heading: Truncation and resolution
resolution.body: A length-N record has frequency spacing fs/N. Truncating shortens the support and widens the main lobe, so closely spaced components merge. Zero-padding interpolates the spectrum but cannot create resolution.

timeScale.heading: Time scaling
timeScale.body: Compressing time by a widens the spectrum by a and shifts every frequency upward. This is the Fourier time-scaling property students see when the extent factor changes.

lanes.heading: Stereo lanes
lanes.body: Both lanes share the operation parameters. Each lane is processed and measured separately, so energy, power and support can differ between channels.

reverse.empty: Select at least two samples to compare spectra.

observe.title: What to observe
observe.reverse: Time reversal keeps the magnitude spectrum; the phase is conjugated plus a linear phase term. It is not reverb.
observe.reverb: Reverb convolves the signal with an impulse response; a longer IR adds a longer tail.
observe.tail: The output keeps the full convolution tail: pre-delay + source length + IR length − 1 samples.
observe.direct: Direct convolution is easy to read but grows with source length × IR length; the FFT path is faster for long inputs.
observe.ir: Changing the IR seed changes the noise detail, not the RT60 decay envelope or the overall energy.
observe.stereo: In stereo mode the impulse response has four paths: direct left/right plus two cross paths. The cross paths decorrelate the channels and widen the image; a mono source cannot enter this mode.

convolution.heading: Reverb as an LTI system
convolution.body: An impulse response records how a room answers one click. Convolving the dry signal with that response adds every reflection at its correct delay and level; fast convolution does the same job through the FFT.

ir.heading: Reading the impulse response
ir.body: The direct sound is the first peak; the tail decay sets RT60, the time for the response to fall by 60 dB. Pre-delay separates the direct sound from the first reflection, and wet/dry sets how much dry signal remains.

direct.heading: Direct versus FFT convolution
direct.body: Direct convolution is easy to inspect but costs O(NL). Overlap-add FFT convolution is O(N log N) and is the default for long IRs. Both must produce the same samples apart from rounding.

stereo.heading: True-stereo four-path reverb
stereo.body: A stereo room answers each source channel into both ears. The matrix applies four convolutions: the diagonal paths LL and RR keep the source on its own side, while RL and LR carry each source into the opposite output. A two-channel IR fills only the diagonal; a four-channel IR stores LL, LR, RL and RR. The built-in cross paths use decorrelated seeds and a fixed 0.5 gain, so the image widens without renormalizing the wet level.

theory.title: Definitions and what to observe
theory.energy: SNR compares signal energy with error energy; MSE averages the squared sample error and is sensitive to outliers.
theory.segmental: Segmental SNR averages per-frame SNR over 20 ms active frames, so a bad short passage is not hidden by a good average.
theory.psnr: PSNR = 10·log10(peak² / MSE) with peak = 1.0 for full-scale float audio.

observe.title: What to observe
observe.lossless: A lossless codec still differs from the float original by 16-bit PCM quantization error; SNR is finite and PSNR is large.
observe.lossy: Lower lossy bitrates raise MSE and lower SNR/PSNR; listen to the same result for the perceptual difference.
observe.bitrate: Compare several codec settings and relate the metric change to the bitrate shown in the compression lab.
observe.body: Use metrics as evidence, not as a verdict: a high SNR does not guarantee that the result sounds clean, and a low SNR can come from one short but important event.

psychoacoustics.description: Explore absolute hearing threshold, critical bands and simultaneous masking, then see why a perceptual codec can discard masked content.
psychoacoustics.noSource: Load audio to overlay measured band levels and the masking threshold. The curves below work without audio.

chart.ath: Absolute threshold of hearing versus frequency
chart.bands: Measured band levels with the masking threshold

status.error: The psychoacoustic analysis failed. Shorten the selection and try again.

ath.heading: Absolute threshold of hearing
ath.body: The Terhardt approximation gives the sound pressure level a pure tone needs to become audible in quiet. Sensitivity peaks near 3–4 kHz and falls sharply at low and very high frequencies; the model is clamped below 20 Hz.

critical.heading: Critical bands
critical.body: The Bark scale warps frequency onto a perceptual axis. The lab uses 25 equal-Bark bands; each band behaves like one auditory filter, so masking spreads mainly between nearby bands.

masking.heading: Simultaneous masking
masking.body: A loud band raises the threshold of neighbouring bands. The model sums masker contributions with a symmetric spreading function and combines the result with the absolute threshold. The strongest masker wins; contributions add on a power basis.

smr.heading: Signal-to-mask ratio
smr.body: SMR is the band level minus its masked threshold. A positive SMR means the band is audible and needs bits; a negative SMR means the band can be quantized coarsely or dropped.

discard.heading: Why codecs discard masked content
discard.body: A perceptual codec derives a per-band quantization step from the masked threshold, never finer than a global rate-control step. Bands under the threshold get coarse steps, so their bits are saved with little audible loss. This model is stationary: it has no temporal masking and no tonal/noise separation, so treat it as a teaching approximation.

asr.intro: Speech recognition runs faster-whisper medium on the first 30 s of the source. The tab shows the transcript, timestamped segments, and — for the bundled speech demo — the word error rate (WER) against its reference transcript. The model is multilingual; CPU transcription takes noticeably longer than a tiny model.

pitchBeat.intro: Pitch and beat analysis is non-neural: librosa estimates F0 with pYIN and tempo with an onset envelope. No model is downloaded or loaded.
pitchBeat.noSource: Load audio to analyse pitch or beats.
pitchBeat.pitchChartNote: Unvoiced frames leave gaps; the vertical axis spans the detected F0 range.

caption.approximation: AI-generated approximation: compare it with the original before drawing conclusions.

concept.heading: How the model suppresses noise
concept.body: The model estimates a time-frequency mask from noisy speech and multiplies it with the complex spectrum. Unlike a fixed high-pass filter, the suppression follows speech and noise patterns learned from data.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Compare the enhanced speech with the noisy demo and listen for the same events.

bullets.noise: Noise between words should drop more than speech onsets.
bullets.artifacts: Listen for musical noise or smeared consonants; over-suppression removes detail.
bullets.shape: The waveform and spectrogram should keep the same duration and sample rate.

pitfalls.heading: Pitfalls and approximation
pitfalls.body: Denoising can improve listening but hurt a downstream recognizer. AI output is an approximation, not a recovered clean recording.

bullets.speechLoss: A high mask can delete weak speech sounds as well as noise.
bullets.notRecovered: Artifacts remain; do not present the result as the original clean source.

concept.heading: Extension versus interpolation
concept.body: Sinc interpolation can only fill between existing samples, while a learned model predicts plausible content above the old Nyquist frequency from the low band.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Compare the learned result with the sinc baseline on the same speech clip.

bullets.spectrum: LavaSR should extend energy above the cutoff; interpolation leaves a hard band edge.
bullets.brightness: Listen for added brightness against a dull, band-limited copy.
bullets.plausibility: Decide whether new high-frequency detail sounds plausible or artificial.

pitfalls.heading: Pitfalls and approximation
pitfalls.body: The model cannot restore information that was never recorded; it invents plausible detail. AI output is an approximation.

bullets.invented: Treat high-band content as generated, not recovered.
bullets.rates: Different sample rates must be mapped back explicitly before listening or measuring.

concept.heading: Separating by time-frequency masks
concept.body: A separator estimates one mask or waveform per stem in the time-frequency domain, then reconstructs each source. The stems add back to an approximation of the mix, not to the exact original tracks.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Solo each stem and then compare their sum with the mix.

bullets.solo: Vocals should dominate the vocal stem and drums the drum stem.
bullets.bleed: Listen for bleed and hollow artifacts where another source was removed.
bullets.sum: The summed stems should resemble the original mix, with some error.

pitfalls.heading: Pitfalls and approximation
pitfalls.body: Separation is not unmixing the original studio tracks; overlap and reverb cause errors. AI output is an approximation.

bullets.notTracks: Do not claim access to the master tracks; the output is estimated.
bullets.excerpt: CPU runs use a short excerpt, so a full-file result is not implied.

concept.heading: Acoustic model, language model, and WER
concept.body: An acoustic model maps frames to text tokens and a language model resolves ambiguous sounds. WER counts substitutions, deletions, and insertions over the reference word count.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Keep the reference transcript fixed while you change the codec setting.

bullets.reference: Compare the transcript with the bundled reference after each codec.
bullets.bitrate: Lower bitrates usually raise WER, but a denoiser can also hurt recognition.
bullets.normalization: The checker normalizes case, punctuation, and whitespace before counting.

pitfalls.heading: Pitfalls and approximation
pitfalls.body: The transcript is an AI approximation, not a guaranteed caption. WER requires an aligned reference and honest normalization.

bullets.alignment: Do not compare raw strings without the documented normalization.
bullets.persian: Tiny models are weak for Persian; use the English speech demo for this experiment.

concept.heading: Residual vector quantization
concept.body: A neural codec encodes the signal as indices into learned codebooks. Residual vector quantization refines the waveform in stages; more stages or larger codebooks raise the bitrate and usually lower distortion.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Move across bitrates and compare decoded audio with the original.

bullets.bitrates: Compare at least low, medium, and high bitrate settings.
bullets.rateDistortion: Watch the neural point against the traditional codec points.
bullets.artifacts: At very low rates the codec keeps structure but loses detail.

pitfalls.heading: Pitfalls and approximation
pitfalls.body: A neural codec is not bit-exact and its delay must be aligned before metrics. Decoded audio is an AI approximation.

bullets.alignment: Align codec delay before computing SNR or PSNR.
bullets.stages: Reported bitrate includes every quantizer stage; do not compare only one.

concept.heading: Frame-wise fundamental frequency
concept.body: pYIN searches candidate periods in short frames and scores how well each candidate explains the waveform. The result is a fundamental-frequency contour with a voiced probability per frame.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Compare the F0 curve with the waveform and spectrogram of the same excerpt.

bullets.contour: A steady vowel or hum should produce a flat F0 segment.
bullets.unvoiced: Noise and many consonants have no stable F0, so the curve breaks.
bullets.octave: Sudden jumps by a factor of two are octave errors, not real pitch changes.

pitfalls.heading: Pitfalls and limits
pitfalls.body: F0 is a physical repetition rate, while perceived pitch also depends on loudness and spectrum. Treat the curve as an estimate.

bullets.range: The search is limited to 65–1000 Hz; notes outside that range are not tracked.
bullets.noise: Broadband noise and polyphonic mixtures rarely give one meaningful F0.

beat.title: Beat tracking: tempo and beat times

concept.heading: Onset envelope and tempo
concept.body: The tracker builds an onset-strength envelope, estimates a global tempo, then places beats on strong onsets that fit that tempo. Tempo in BPM is 60 divided by the average beat period.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Listen to the excerpt while checking where the beat list falls.

bullets.tempo: A steady pulse near 120 BPM should produce a tempo close to 120.
bullets.list: Beat times must increase and match audible attacks.
bullets.speech: Speech has no fixed musical meter, so its tempo estimate can be unstable.

pitfalls.heading: Pitfalls and limits
pitfalls.body: Beat tracking assumes a roughly periodic pulse. Tempo can double or halve when the meter is ambiguous.

bullets.meter: A 60 BPM pulse and a 120 BPM pulse can share the same onsets; check the beat count.
bullets.cut: The 30 s excerpt can cut a phrase, so the first and last beats deserve less trust.

concept.heading: From spectrogram patches to labels
concept.body: AST turns the log-mel spectrogram into overlapping patches and applies a transformer encoder. A linear head produces one logit per AudioSet class; a sigmoid turns each logit into an independent score.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Use a short excerpt with one clear sound source, then compare the top labels with what you hear.

bullets.overlap: Several labels can be high at once: a music clip may also score singing, speech or instruments.
bullets.windows: Averaging 10 s windows makes the score stable; a short event can disappear under a long steady background.
bullets.domain: The model knows AudioSet classes only. Sounds outside that vocabulary are forced into the nearest class.

pitfalls.heading: Common pitfalls
pitfalls.body: A high score is not a detection guarantee and a missing label is not proof of absence.

bullets.taxonomy: The labels are the English AudioSet taxonomy; translation would change the classes, so the UI keeps the original names.
bullets.notCaption: Classification is not speech recognition or audio captioning: it returns class scores, not words or descriptions.

classification.intro: Fine-tuned Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) scores the excerpt against the 527 AudioSet classes. The backend averages independent sigmoid scores over non-overlapping 10 s windows; the result is a ranked approximation, not a caption.
classification.modelMissing: The AST model is not downloaded. Fetch it with the command below, then reload.
classification.noSource: Load audio, or use the music demo, to classify the excerpt.
classification.empty: The model returned no labels for this excerpt.
classification.taxonomyNote: Labels come from AudioSet’s English taxonomy and are not translated. Scores are independent, so they do not sum to 100%.

lane.linked: Right lane mirrors the left lane.

error.invalid: The cutoff must lie inside (0, Nyquist). Check the cutoff, band edges, order, taps, and ripple.
error.designFailed: Filter design failed. Check the parameters and try again.
error.playback: The filtered result does not fit the playback caps.
error.applyFailed: Applying the filter failed. Try a shorter excerpt.

filters.delayNote: A linear-phase FIR reports and compensates its group delay for preview alignment. The causal IIR response is not trimmed.
filters.unstableWarning: This design is unstable (a pole lies outside the unit circle); apply is disabled.

plots.empty: Not enough finite data to draw this plot.

poleZero.title: Pole-zero plane
poleZero.aria: Pole-zero plot with the unit circle
poleZero.omitted: Roots are omitted for FIR designs above 33 taps.

transfer.heading: Transfer function
transfer.body: A linear time-invariant filter is described by a rational transfer function in z. The roots of the numerator are zeros and the roots of the denominator are poles.

fir.heading: FIR window method
fir.body: Sample the ideal response and truncate it with a window. A wider window narrows the transition band; a smoother window lowers the side lobes.

butterworth.heading: Butterworth response
butterworth.body: Butterworth is maximally flat in the passband and steepens as the order rises.

chebyshev.heading: Chebyshev type I response
chebyshev.body: Chebyshev type I accepts small passband ripple to get a sharper transition at the same order.

groupDelay.heading: Group delay
groupDelay.body: Group delay is the derivative of phase with frequency; it describes the delay of a narrow-band envelope, not the phase delay of each sinusoid.

poles.heading: Poles and stability
poles.body: Inside the unit circle is stable, outside is unstable, and on the circle is marginal. A pole closer to the circle produces a sharper resonance and slower decay.

lanes.heading: Per-lane filters
lanes.body: A linked pair applies one design to both playback lanes. Unlink the pair to give each lane its own cutoff or design; the response and pole-zero plots show the selected lane. Independent filtering can widen, narrow, or shift the stereo image.

observe.heading: What to observe
observe.body: Change one control at a time and compare these four effects.

bullets.cutoff: Cutoff sets the edge; the transition width depends on the order or the FIR tap count and window.
bullets.order: Higher order or a longer FIR gives a steeper transition but more ringing near the edge.
bullets.linearPhase: A symmetric FIR has linear phase; the price is a delay of about (taps − 1) / 2 samples.
bullets.poles: Poles near the unit circle produce a visible resonance and a longer impulse response.

pitfalls.heading: Common pitfalls
pitfalls.body: These three mistakes cause most confusion.

bullets.nyquist: A cutoff at or above Nyquist is invalid; the design is rejected.
bullets.unstable: An IIR design with a pole outside the unit circle is unstable and must not be applied.
bullets.delay: Phase delay and group delay are not the same; check the group-delay plot, not only the phase plot.

theory.title: Pipeline theory and what to observe

stereo.heading: Stereo lanes
stereo.body: With both lanes selected the same validated graph runs once per lane. Outputs combine only when rate and length match, so a graph that changes lanes differently is refused instead of silently misaligned.

sampling.heading: Sampling and aliasing
sampling.body: A resample block changes the sample rate. If the anti-alias filter is off, content above the new Nyquist frequency folds back as an alias; the graph shows the same trade-off as the sampling lab.

filtering.heading: Filtering
filtering.body: A filter block applies a difference equation. FIR blocks use only inputs, so they have linear phase and a fixed delay; IIR blocks reuse outputs, so a small order gives a sharp transition but a non-linear phase.

quantization.heading: Quantization
quantization.body: A quantize block rounds each sample to N bits. The step is 2A/2^N and the ideal full-scale sine SNR is about 6.02N + 1.76 dB; dither trades a little added noise for removed correlation between the error and the signal.

codec.heading: Codec branch
codec.body: A codec block encodes and immediately decodes the branch. Lossless blocks return bit-exact audio; the MDCT block quantizes spectral coefficients, so its bit budget controls the artifact level.

reverb.heading: Reverb
reverb.body: A reverb block convolves the branch with an impulse response. The output keeps the full tail, so it is longer than the input; the wet/dry mix and pre-delay set the balance and the gap before the first reflection.

timeStretch.heading: Time-stretch
timeStretch.body: A time-stretch block changes duration while keeping pitch. The phase vocoder shifts the frame grid, unlike resampling, where speed and pitch move together.

order.heading: Order effects
order.body: Order matters. Reversing after a filter is not the same as filtering a reversed signal, and a quantizer before a codec removes detail the codec can never recover.

fanOut.heading: Why fan-out helps
fanOut.body: Fan-out sends the same input into parallel branches. Each output is an independent experiment on the same excerpt, so a filter branch and a codec branch can be compared side by side.

theory.title: Theory and what to observe
theory.stereoNote: Analysis runs on a mono downmix for comparability. Playback and real codecs preserve stereo.

experiments.title: Guided experiments
experiments.intro: Each card is a short lab sheet. Open the linked lab, change one control at a time, and compare what you hear and see with the expected observation.

filters.title: Filter design: cutoff, order, and group delay
filters.goal: See how cutoff, order, ripple, and topology change the transition band, ringing, and group delay.

s1.instruction: Load the chirp demo and design an FIR low-pass with 101 taps at 4 kHz using a Hamming window.
s1.observation: With 101 taps the transition is wide and the magnitude rolls off around 4 kHz.

s2.instruction: Switch to Butterworth with order 8 and keep the same cutoff.
s2.observation: A higher order narrows the transition but adds ringing near the edge.

s3.instruction: Switch to Chebyshev type I with order 8 and 0.5 dB ripple.
s3.observation: Passband ripple appears, and the group delay peaks near the cutoff.

s4.instruction: Return to FIR and read the group-delay and impulse-response plots.
s4.observation: The symmetric FIR has a flat group delay away from the transition.

s5.instruction: Switch to a high-pass FIR at 2 kHz with 101 taps.
s5.observation: Low frequencies fall and the transition width follows the tap count.

s6.instruction: Design a Butterworth band-pass from 1 to 3 kHz, order 4.
s6.observation: Only the middle band survives; the order controls both edges.

s7.instruction: Change the band-pass to a band-stop with the same edges.
s7.observation: The middle band is removed while the low and high sides remain.

s8.instruction: Design a peaking biquad at 1 kHz with +6 dB gain and Q = 1, then read the pole-zero plot.
s8.observation: The poles stay inside the unit circle, so the filter is stable; the peak sits at 1 kHz.

waveformSpectrogram.title: Waveform and spectrogram: same sound, two views
waveformSpectrogram.goal: Connect the time-domain envelope with the time–frequency picture and see how analysis settings change what is visible.

s1.instruction: Load the chirp demo and open the waveform lab.
s1.observation: The overview shows a five-second envelope, and the header reports the sample count and rate.

s2.instruction: Zoom into the first 100 ms, then keep zooming until individual samples appear.
s2.observation: The envelope becomes discrete points; read exact times from the numeric selection readout, not from pixel position.

s3.instruction: Select about half a second across the rising chirp and open the spectrogram on the same range.
s3.observation: The spectrogram shows one rising ridge; the selection is the analysis window.

s4.instruction: Compare spectrogram windows of 256, 1024, and 4096 samples.
s4.observation: The short window localises time but smears frequency; the long window does the opposite.

s5.instruction: Zero-pad the FFT while keeping the same window length.
s5.observation: The ridge looks smoother and the grid finer, but its width does not shrink: zero-padding interpolates, it does not add resolution.

sampling.title: Sampling rate, aliasing, and bit depth
sampling.goal: Hear and see aliasing, then measure how bit depth and dither change the quantization noise floor.

s1.instruction: Load the chirp demo and resample from 48 kHz to 8 kHz with the anti-alias filter off.
s1.observation: The sweep folds: high tones return as lower tones and the spectrogram shows mirror images.

s2.instruction: Turn the anti-alias filter on and repeat.
s2.observation: Energy above 4 kHz disappears before decimation, so no folded ridge remains.

s3.instruction: Keep 8 kHz and reduce bit depth from 16 to 8 bits without dither.
s3.observation: A noise floor rises and SNR falls by roughly the expected 6 dB per bit.

s4.instruction: Keep 8 kHz and reduce to 4 bits with TPDF dither on.
s4.observation: The error becomes noise-like instead of correlated with the signal; the sound is noisier but less buzzy.

s5.instruction: Measure SNR at 16, 12, 8, and 4 bits and compare with 6.02N + 1.76 dB.
s5.observation: Each four-bit drop costs about 24 dB; the measured value stays a little below the full-scale-sine bound.

extent.title: Signal extent: duration, energy, and resolution
extent.goal: Relate support and duration to energy, power, and the frequency resolution of a finite record.

s1.instruction: Load a short clip and read duration, sample count, support, energy, and average power in the extent lab.
s1.observation: The support is the non-zero region and can be shorter than the file.

s2.instruction: Truncate the signal to 12000 samples (0.25 s at 48 kHz).
s2.observation: Energy drops and the spectrum's main lobe widens; the time–bandwidth product resists compression.

s3.instruction: Keep the first 12000 samples and zero-pad them with another 12000 zeros.
s3.observation: The curve is sampled more finely, but no new detail appears between the original bins.

s4.instruction: Shift the signal by 0.1 s (4800 samples at 48 kHz).
s4.observation: The waveform moves in time and the phase changes linearly while the magnitude stays unchanged.

s5.observation: Time reversal conjugates the phase spectrum but leaves the magnitude spectrum unchanged.

s6.instruction: Scale time by 0.5 and compare the spectrum with the original.
s6.observation: The waveform is compressed and the spectrum stretched by two, demonstrating x(at).

fft.title: DFT: windows, leakage, phase, and algorithms
fft.goal: Read a spectrum carefully, then compare our FFT with a reference library and inspect the butterflies.

s1.instruction: Select a steady tone segment and open the Fourier view with a Hann window of 1024 samples.
s1.observation: The peak sits at the tone frequency and the window sets the lobe shape.

s2.instruction: Switch to a rectangular window and keep the same length.
s2.observation: The main lobe narrows but side lobes rise: leakage becomes obvious.

s3.instruction: Try a Blackman window at 4096 samples.
s3.observation: Side lobes fall far below the rectangular case while the main lobe widens.

s4.instruction: Return to Hann and increase the window length to 8192 samples.
s4.observation: The main lobe narrows and close tones resolve better, at the cost of time resolution.

s5.instruction: Switch phase to unwrapped with a −80 dB mask.
s5.observation: Bins below the mask disappear, and the surviving phase is easier to follow.

s6.instruction: Compare linear and dB magnitude on the same frame.
s6.observation: dB exposes low-level components; linear keeps the relative amplitude intuitive.

s7.instruction: Run the FFT benchmark against the reference library.
s7.observation: Both transforms agree within tolerance while the timings show the cost of the educational path.

s8.instruction: Step through the N = 8 butterfly view.
s8.observation: Each stage halves the number of independent transforms, and the replay matches the full FFT.

spectrumEdit.title: Spectrum editing: magnitude, phase, and the return to time
spectrumEdit.goal: Edit one frame in the frequency domain and hear what each representation does and does not preserve.

s1.instruction: Load a tone and inspect Re, Im, magnitude, and phase for one frame.
s1.observation: The tone occupies a few bins; phase elsewhere is mostly numerical noise.

s2.instruction: Zero the imaginary part with Hermitian symmetry on.
s2.observation: The inverse stays real and the waveform becomes symmetric in a predictable way.

s3.instruction: Set every phase to zero while keeping magnitude.
s3.observation: The result is a concentrated pulse; phase alignment creates the sharp peak.

s4.instruction: Keep magnitude only and randomise phase.
s4.observation: Energy is preserved but the waveform turns noise-like; magnitude alone does not determine the sound.

s5.instruction: Keep phase only and set magnitude to one.
s5.observation: The reconstruction keeps temporal structure but loses the spectral envelope.

s6.instruction: Draw a brick-wall zero over a band and apply the IFFT.
s6.observation: The edited band disappears and ripples appear around it.

s7.instruction: Turn Hermitian symmetry off and repeat the band edit.
s7.observation: The IFFT becomes complex; the player keeps the real part, which is an explicit approximation.

s8.instruction: Listen to the brick-wall result and then smooth the mask edges.
s8.observation: Sharp edges ring; a gradual transition reduces the Gibbs ripple.

speed.title: Speed: resampling versus phase-vocoder stretching
speed.goal: Separate tempo from pitch and see why reverse is not the same operation as reverb.

s1.instruction: Set resampling speed to 2× and play the result.
s1.observation: Duration halves and pitch rises by an octave; the spectrogram shifts upward.

s2.instruction: Switch to time-stretch at 2× with the same excerpt.
s2.observation: Duration halves while the spectral ridges stay at the same frequencies.

s3.observation: The sound slows and drops an octave; this is the tape effect.

s4.instruction: Use pitch shift of +12 semitones with duration preserved.
s4.observation: Pitch doubles while the timeline stays fixed, the opposite trade from resampling.

s5.observation: The envelope flips in time; magnitude is unchanged while phase is conjugated.

reverb.title: Reverse and reverb: two different operations
reverb.goal: Treat reverb as convolution with an impulse response and keep time reversal conceptually separate.

s1.instruction: Load the chirp demo and choose the synthetic hall impulse response.
s1.observation: The IR shows an early direct peak and a decaying tail; its spectrum colours the result.

s2.instruction: Raise the hall RT60 from 1.8 s to 3 s.
s2.observation: The tail lengthens and the spectrogram shows energy persisting after the dry sound ends.

s3.instruction: Choose the plate preset and raise the wet mix.
s3.observation: The density and brightness change; wet/dry controls how much dry signal survives.

s4.observation: A silent gap separates the direct sound from the first reflection.

s5.instruction: Switch from FFT to direct convolution on a short excerpt.
s5.observation: The samples match apart from rounding, while the timing shows why overlap-add is the default for long IRs.

generatorFourier.title: Fourier series and Gibbs ringing
generatorFourier.goal: Build a periodic wave harmonic by harmonic and watch convergence, overshoot, and ripple width.

s1.instruction: Generate a square wave with one harmonic.
s1.observation: The result is a pure sine at the fundamental.

s2.instruction: Raise the harmonic count to three.
s2.observation: The edges steepen and the waveform begins to resemble a square.

s3.instruction: Raise the count to nine and watch the edges.
s3.observation: Ripples appear near every jump: the Gibbs overshoot.

s4.observation: The ripple width shrinks but the overshoot stays near 9% of the jump.

s5.instruction: Switch the target to a triangle wave with fifteen harmonics.
s5.observation: A triangle converges faster because its coefficients fall as 1/k².

codecLab.title: Compression: lossless, lossy, and real codecs
codecLab.goal: Compare entropy coding, companding, transform coding, and an ffmpeg codec on the same excerpt.

s1.instruction: Encode the chirp excerpt with RLE.
s1.observation: RLE barely compresses ordinary audio because equal-byte runs are rare.

s2.instruction: Encode with canonical Huffman and compare the size with entropy.
s2.observation: The code approaches the entropy bound but cannot beat it.

s3.observation: Prediction shrinks the symbol range and the file gets smaller than plain Huffman.

s4.observation: The result is not bit-exact; quiet detail is preserved at the cost of coarse large samples.

s5.observation: The envelope survives but fine detail smears and SNR drops.

s6.observation: Artifacts weaken and the rate–distortion point moves up.

s7.observation: Quality approaches transparency while the bitrate cost grows.

s8.instruction: Encode the same excerpt with MP3 at 128 kbps and compare after alignment.
s8.observation: The decoded result is delayed; metrics must align it before comparing.

metrics.title: Quality metrics: SNR, segmental SNR, and PSNR
metrics.goal: Read metrics as evidence and learn when alignment or framing makes a number meaningless.

s1.instruction: Process a clip with any lab and open the metrics view.
s1.observation: Metrics compare the original with the processed lane; unmatched lengths or rates show a hint instead of a number.

s2.instruction: Apply a lossless Huffman round trip and read the metrics.
s2.observation: SNR is finite because the source is float and the codec path stores 16-bit PCM; PSNR is large.

s3.observation: Lower bitrate raises MSE and lowers SNR and PSNR.

s4.instruction: Compare plain SNR with segmental SNR on a clip with one loud click.
s4.observation: Segmental SNR reacts to the short bad frame while the global average dilutes it.

s5.instruction: Try to compare signals with different sample rates.
s5.observation: The view refuses to align them silently; resample or re-encode first.

aiSeparation.title: Source separation: stems and masks
aiSeparation.goal: Run a four-stem model on a short excerpt, judge bleed and artifacts, and see the CPU cost.

s1.instruction: Load the mixed music demo and open the separation task.
s1.observation: The original is mono-downmixed for analysis, but stereo playback remains available.

s2.observation: The model reports the target stems: vocals, drums, bass, and other.

s3.instruction: Run the default 30-second excerpt and watch progress.
s3.observation: The job reports progress and can be cancelled; CPU timing is slower than real time.

s4.observation: The lead voice is emphasised, but bleed from other instruments remains.

s5.observation: Transients and low end separate more cleanly than reverberant content.

s6.instruction: Listen for artifacts at stem boundaries.
s6.observation: Neural separation can smear attacks and leave musical noise; it is an approximation.

s7.instruction: Run the whole file and compare the ETA.
s7.observation: Longer input costs proportionally more; the excerpt limit exists for the local demo.

s8.instruction: Sum the stems and compare with the original mix.
s8.observation: The reconstruction is close but not exact; masks are estimated, not inverted exactly.

aiDenoise.title: Denoising: learned suppression
aiDenoise.goal: Compare a learned mask with a fixed filter and check whether denoising helps or hurts later tasks.

s1.instruction: Load the noisy speech demo and inspect the spectrogram.
s1.observation: Noise fills the gaps between words across the whole band.

s2.observation: The output duration and rate match the input; only the spectral envelope changes.

s3.observation: Stationary noise drops more than speech onsets.

s4.observation: Over-suppression can smear /s/ and /f/; denoising is not free.

s5.instruction: Try a music clip with the same speech model.
s5.observation: Out-of-domain input can be damaged; the model is trained for speech.

s6.instruction: Compare the enhanced waveform with the noisy one.
s6.observation: The noise floor falls while speech peaks stay roughly in place.

s7.instruction: Run ASR on noisy and denoised speech.
s7.observation: Denoising can help or hurt recognition; measure rather than assume.

s8.instruction: Read the model caption and limitations.
s8.observation: The result is an AI approximation, not a mathematically exact filter.

aiSuperres.title: Super-resolution: bandwidth extension
aiSuperres.goal: Separate restoring a sample rate from inventing high-frequency content on speech.

s1.instruction: Load the speech demo and inspect its spectrum.
s1.observation: The original fills the band supported by its sample rate.

s2.instruction: Band-limit a copy to 8 kHz and inspect the edge at 4 kHz.
s2.observation: The low-pass leaves a hard spectral edge and no energy above it.

s3.instruction: Restore the sample rate with the sinc path.
s3.observation: The rate returns but the 4 kHz edge remains; sinc invents no high-band content.

s4.instruction: Switch the restore path to the neural model.
s4.observation: The model adds energy above 4 kHz that the band-limited input did not contain.

s5.instruction: Compare the neural and sinc spectra above 4 kHz.
s5.observation: The neural result looks fuller; decide whether the detail is plausible or artificial.

s6.observation: Extension can brighten speech but may add lisping or unnatural hiss.

s7.observation: Results vary with content; speech models are not general audio restorers.

s8.observation: Super-resolution is an estimate, not recovered ground truth.

aiAsr.title: Automatic speech recognition and WER
aiAsr.goal: Measure recognition quality, compute WER, and read the trade-offs of a multilingual model.

s1.instruction: Load the speech demo and open the ASR task.
s1.observation: The bundled demo is English, so the shipped reference transcript enables WER; the model can also transcribe Persian without a reference.

s2.observation: The job returns text with timestamps and the model label; CPU jobs may take tens of seconds for the 30 s excerpt.

s3.instruction: Read the transcript against the known demo sentence.
s3.observation: Substitutions and missing words are visible; compare case-insensitively.

s4.instruction: Compare the transcript with the reference sentence.
s4.observation: Read substitutions, deletions and insertions; WER normalization ignores case.

s5.instruction: Compute WER from substitutions, deletions, and insertions.
s5.observation: WER = (S + D + I) / N; one missed word can dominate a short clip.

s6.instruction: Try the same speech after heavy compression.
s6.observation: This lab reads the original source; use the codec lab to hear the compressed version and discuss the mismatch.

s7.instruction: Transcribe a Persian excerpt when one is available.
s7.observation: Medium supports Persian, but no bundled Persian reference exists, so WER stays hidden.

s8.instruction: Record CPU time for the excerpt.
s8.observation: Medium trades speed for multilingual accuracy; choose the smallest model that meets the task.

aiNeuralCodec.title: Neural codec: RVQ and rate–distortion
aiNeuralCodec.goal: Compare a learned codec with MDCT and read the bitrate–quality trade without hype.

s1.instruction: Load the speech demo and open the neural-codec task.
s1.observation: The model expects a fixed sample rate and resamples explicitly.

s2.instruction: Run EnCodec on a short excerpt.
s2.observation: The output is decoded audio plus a reported bitrate.

s3.observation: Speech remains intelligible even at low bitrate, with characteristic coding artifacts.

s4.observation: The neural codec spends bits on learned features rather than waveform samples.

s5.instruction: Compare with MDCT at a similar bitrate.
s5.observation: The two codecs fail differently; listen and check the metrics.

s6.observation: Lower bitrate trades quality for size, as with classical codecs.

s7.observation: Neural codecs can blur attacks and over-smooth noise.

s8.instruction: Read the model license and limitations.
s8.observation: Weights and code have separate terms; record them before deployment.

aiPitchBeat.title: Pitch and beat tracking
aiPitchBeat.goal: Read an F0 curve and a tempo estimate, and learn what these signal-processing trackers assume.

s1.instruction: Load a sustained tone or the click demo and open the pitch task.
s1.observation: Analysis jobs run even when the ML service is disabled because they use librosa, not a neural model.

s2.observation: The result is an F0 curve in Hz with time stamps.

s3.instruction: Compare the curve with the generator frequency.
s3.observation: A clean sine gives a flat track; silence and noise produce gaps or jumps.

s4.observation: The excerpt limit and the current selection control the analysed range.

s5.instruction: Switch to the beat task on a click train.
s5.observation: The result lists tempo and beat times rather than a pitch curve.

s6.observation: A 120 BPM click train should land near 120, within the tracker's tolerance.

s7.observation: Beat tracking follows the dominant pulse; ambiguous rhythms can halve or double the tempo.

s8.observation: pyin and beat tracking are signal-processing methods with parameters, not trained models.

pipeline.title: Pipeline: composition and order
pipeline.goal: Chain blocks, inspect intermediate results, and see why order and lossy stages matter.

s1.instruction: Open the pipeline lab and add a resample node.
s1.observation: Each block is a pure function of its input and parameters.

s2.observation: The chain applies resample then filter; the intermediate signal can be inspected.

s3.instruction: Append a quantizer and choose 8 bits.
s3.observation: Quantization noise appears after filtering, not before.

s4.instruction: Add an MDCT codec block at a low bitrate.
s4.observation: The codec removes detail that later blocks cannot restore.

s5.instruction: Add a reverb block with a synthetic IR.
s5.observation: Convolution runs last in this chain and lengthens the output.

s6.instruction: Swap the filter and reverse blocks.
s6.observation: The result changes because convolution and time reversal do not commute.

s7.instruction: Fan out the same input into two branches.
s7.observation: Each branch is an independent experiment on the same excerpt.

s8.observation: Metrics show where quality is lost; composition is not associative in practice when blocks are lossy.

psychoacoustics.title: Psychoacoustics: thresholds, Bark bands, and masking
psychoacoustics.goal: Read the absolute threshold and masking curves, then connect them to perceptual coding.

s1.instruction: Open the lab with no audio and read the absolute threshold curve.
s1.observation: The threshold is lowest around 2–5 kHz and rises at both extremes.

s2.observation: Bands are wider at high frequencies; masking spreads differently across the basilar membrane.

s3.observation: The whole threshold and masking overlay shifts with the assumed playback level.

s4.instruction: Load the tone demo and switch to a linear frequency axis.
s4.observation: Linear spacing makes low-frequency detail easier to see; log spacing matches hearing better.

s5.instruction: Read the measured band levels over the masking threshold.
s5.observation: Bands below the threshold are candidates for removal by a perceptual codec.

s6.instruction: Compare a tonal masker with a noise masker.
s6.observation: Noise masks a wider range; tonal masking is more local in frequency.

s7.instruction: Connect the result to the MDCT codec.
s7.observation: The toy codec uses a simple masking model; real codecs use finer psychoacoustic models.

s8.observation: The model is illustrative, not a certified perceptual standard.
